steps.title: Recognize repeated subproblems
steps.content: Dynamic programming (DP) solves a problem by reusing results of smaller subproblems instead of recalculating them. It is useful when subproblems overlap and an optimal solution can be built from optimal smaller solutions.
steps.example: Naive recursive Fibonacci recalculates fib(2) many times.

steps.title: Choose a DP signal
steps.prompt: Which property suggests that dynamic programming may help?
steps.explanation: DP saves work when the same smaller subproblems are solved repeatedly.

steps.title: Memoization versus tabulation
steps.content: Memoization is top-down: solve recursively and store each result. Tabulation is bottom-up: fill a table from base cases toward the answer.
steps.example: For Fibonacci, store fib(0), fib(1), then compute each next value once.

steps.title: Find Fibonacci
steps.prompt: Using fib(0)=0 and fib(1)=1, what is fib(5)?

steps.title: Define the state and transition
steps.content: A DP solution needs a state (what a subproblem represents), a transition (how states depend on smaller states), base cases and an evaluation order.
steps.tip: Before writing code, write the meaning of dp[i] in one sentence.

questions.explanation: Memoization stores previously computed results for reuse.
Tabulation computes smaller states first and fills the table toward the final state.

questions.prompt: Which two properties commonly support DP?
questions.explanation: DP benefits from repeated subproblems and solutions built from smaller optimal solutions.

questions.prompt: With fib(0)=0 and fib(1)=1, what is fib(6)?
What should a DP state clearly define?
options: What each stored subproblem value means
questions.explanation: A precise state definition makes the recurrence and base cases understandable.
